part.distant.title: Distant opposition
part.distant.summary: After your move, leave an odd number of squares between the kings: the opposition is yours. The king goes ahead with it; the pawn advances later.
part.lateral.title: Lateral opposition
part.lateral.summary: On the same rank the count is the same: an odd number of squares between the kings, after your move, leaves the opposition with you.
part.capablanca.title: Capablanca's example
part.capablanca.summary: The side to move leaves an odd number of squares between the kings; if the other king changes file, wait and take the opposition back before moving up.
part.edge.title: Lateral approach
part.edge.summary: Going straight for the pawn can hand over the opposition. Step away: the other king cannot use the squares your pawns watch.
ex.e09: Play White and find the best move. Your king starts in the corner, far from the d2-pawn: bring it over with the distant opposition.
ex.e09.hint: First take your king to the black king's file, leaving an odd number of squares between them. Then, after each of his moves, keep the count.
ex.e09.solution:
1.Kg2! takes distant opposition on the g-file, with five squares between the kings. After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf3! maintains opposition on the f-file, now with three intervening squares.

A continuation using the technique studied: 2...Ke6 3.Ke4 Kd6 4.Kd4. The kings reach direct opposition, on the pawn's file and in front of it. If White started with the pawn or with another king move, Black would draw.

1.d4? and 1.d3? advance the pawn with the king in the corner: the black king gets in front of it first. 2.Kf2? leaves four squares, an even number, and the black king holds with 2...Ke6.
ex.e11: Play Black and find the best move. The white pawn is on c2 and the white king on f1. Your king must stop him from reaching the pawn's key squares: b4, c4 and d4.
ex.e11.hint: Take your king to the white king's file and leave an odd number of squares between them. When he changes file, do the same.
ex.e11.solution: 1...Kf7! Kings on f1 and f7, five squares between them, White to move: the distant opposition is yours. After 2.Ke2, 2...Ke6!, with three squares; after 3.Kd2, 3...Kd6!, again with three. The white king never reaches b4, c4 and d4. 1...Kf8? leaves six squares, an even number, and White takes the opposition; 3...Kd5? leaves two, and the white king goes to d3.
ex.e13: Play White and find the best move. The white pawn is on c2, and both kings are far from it.
ex.e13.hint: Before advancing the pawn, leave an odd number of squares between the kings, with Black to move, and bring your king closer to the key squares.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Ke7! The kings stand on the seventh rank, with b7, c7 and d7 between them and Black to move: the lateral opposition is yours. After 1...Kb6, 2.Kd6! leaves only c6 between them, and the white king goes on to the key squares b4, c4 and d4. 1.c3? and 1.c4? advance the pawn before the king, and the black king reaches the new key squares first. 1.Kg7? also leaves an odd number, but takes the king away from the key squares. 2.Ke6? leaves two squares, and the black king goes to c5.
key.lesson: The white king takes the opposition from far away, with several squares between the kings, and closes the gap step by step until it reaches the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.capablanca: {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}}'s example: pawns facing each other, unable to advance, and the kings far apart. Whoever is to move takes the distant opposition and wins.
history:
Opposition is the contest between kings to force the opponent to give up space; it can begin at a distance or along a diagonal. The goal is to reach an important square, capture a pawn, or prevent an opposing entry. In his 1921 book Chess Fundamentals, {{José Raúl Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} explains the topic as an author through pawn-ending examples.

The technique also appears in games: at {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017, {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, playing Black, defended an ending a pawn down against {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, playing White. The black king followed the white king from a distance, and the game ended in a draw. Just a few pieces can conceal a precise contest for space and time.
practice: Now the real ending: king on h3, pawn on f3 and the black king on e6, eyeing the key squares e5, f5 and g5. Win the opposition on the diagonal, turn it into direct opposition and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
ex.e09.r1: 1...Kf7. The black king leaves the g-file and heads for the centre, towards e6 and d5, in front of the d2-pawn. If the white king does not follow it with the distant opposition on the new file, Black takes it, and the pawn does not get through.
ex.e11.r1: 2.Ke2. The white king changes file, heading for the key squares.
ex.e11.r2: 3.Kd2. The white king changes file again.
ex.e13.r1: 1...Kb6. The black king comes down towards the key squares b4, c4 and d4.
title: Distant opposition
summary: Taking the opposition from afar, with an odd number of squares between the kings, to reach the key squares, protect the pawn and keep the enemy king out.
ex.e18: Play White and find the best move. The pawns on the c and h files cannot advance, and the kings are on the same file.
ex.e18.hint: First, take the opposition in a straight line. Then take your king to the pawn the black king has stopped defending.
ex.e18.solution: 1.Ke4! leaves a single square between the kings, e5, with Black to move: the opposition is yours. After 1...Kd6, the black king moves away from the h5-pawn, and 2.Kf5 (or 2.Kf4) takes your king to it. 1.Kf4? lets the black king go to f6, facing yours, and Black draws; 2.Kd3? gives the opposition back.
ex.e18.r1: 1...Kd6. The black king goes towards the c5-pawn and leaves the h5-pawn undefended.
ex.e19: Play as White and find the best move. The a-file pawns are locked and the black king is more active. Your king must reach the other side in time.
ex.e19.hint: It is a race: your king must go to meet the black king through the centre, without losing time, to get counterplay.
ex.e19.solution: 1.Kd7! starts the race against the black king. After 1...Kc5, 2.Ke6! heads for the centre; after 2...Kc4, 3.Ke5 (3.Kf5 also works) and, after 3...Kc3, 4.Ke4! Your king arrives in time to defend and to attack the enemy pawn, and the draw is secured.
ex.e19.r1: 1...Kc5. The black king rushes to the centre and to the side of the a-file pawns.
ex.e19.r2: 2...Kc4. The black king drops another rank, threatening to enter on the queenside.
ex.e19.r3: 3...Kc3. The black king reaches c3 and threatens to go to b2 to attack the a2 pawn.
coach.allPartsDone: Now you know how to win the opposition and take your king to the key squares. Shall we go to the final test?
part.means.title: Choose the target
part.means.summary: Taking the opposition is not the goal: if your king can reach one of the pawn’s key squares directly, go there, even without the opposition.
key.means: The opposition is a means, not the goal: here taking it only draws. What wins is taking the king straight to the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
ex.e22: Play White and find the best move. The pawns are locked: neither side can pass the move with them.
ex.e22.hint: Count the squares between the kings on the sixth rank, the pawn's square included. Also see which square the d4-pawn watches.
ex.e22.solution: 1.Kc6! leaves only d6 between the kings, the pawn's square: one square, an odd number, with Black to move. The black king has to leave e6, and the only square that would hold d5 and d6 at the same time, e5, is watched by the d4-pawn. He backs off, and your king advances: after 1...Ke7, 2.Kb5 goes for the a4-pawn (2.Kc7 also wins; 2.Kxd5? lets the black king go to d7 and draw). If Black plays 1...Kf5, against the d4-pawn, 2.Kxd5 defends the pawn and then captures the d6-pawn. 1.Kb5? and 1.Ka5? go for the a4-pawn too early: the black king runs to f5 and e4, against the d4-pawn, and draws. 1.Ka6? also leaves an odd number of squares, but far from the pawns: the black king runs to f5 and e4.
ex.e21: Play White and find the best move. The white pawn is on f3, and your king is next to it.
ex.e21.hint: The pawn's key squares are e5, f5 and g5. Ask yourself what matters more here: heading for the black king or getting close to those squares.
ex.e21.solution: 1.Kf4! takes the king close to e5, f5 and g5, and the black king cannot guard all three: after 1...Ke7, the white king enters a key square, as in 2.Kf5. 1.Ke4? heads for the black king, and he, on e6, guards e5 and f5: it is a draw. 1.Kd3? takes the king away from the key squares, and the black king, going to e7, arrives in time to guard them: it is a draw. 1.f4? advances the pawn before the king, and the key squares move up to e6, f6 and g6, near the black king. The opposition is a means; the goal is the key square.
